deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivation. It holds methodological notes on the foundations of mathematics: an outline comparing two approaches. The surrounding notebook pages (the next page mentions the planned '24th problem' of the Paris lecture) place it around 1899-1901. It is essentially a sketch of the contrast between the 'genetic' and 'axiomatic' methods that Hilbert published in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (Jahresber. DMV 8, 1900). Reconstructed outline (readings marked [?] are uncertain):

Question: 'What are the foundations of our science?'
(1) Arithmetic: the theory of irrational numbers of Dedekind, Weierstrass and Cantor.
(2) Euclidean geometry.
The two are of equal standing and can replace one another. They are not essentially different in substance, only in the manner of presentation.

(1) proceeds genetically. The transcription reads 'geometrische'; the image and the context strongly suggest 'genetisch'.
(2) proceeds axiomatically. The transcription reads 'analytisch'; 'axiomatisch' fits the hand and the argument better.
There is a marginal remark that something (rigour or analysis?) replaced intuition ('Anschauung') in the 18th century. It comes with an illustrative limit example roughly of the form lim_{x->0,y->0} (1/?)(f(x,y) - f(x',y')) and lim f(x,y) = c. This is presumably a stock example of a double or iterated limit where naive intuition misleads. The formula is too fragmentary to reconstruct with certainty. My guess is that it concerns the interchange of limits or partial derivatives, a standard 19th-century warning example.

Assessment of each method:
(1) gives the 'non plus ultra' of all rigour (the transcription's 'Maass plus ultra' should read 'Non plus ultra').
(2) is essentially the old geometric method, which the ancient mathematicians followed unconsciously; hence it is not inadequate.

Existence of numbers:
(1) asks what 0, 1, ... are, and constructs them.
(2) posits 0, 1 and the axioms; existence must then be proved.

Which way deserves preference? (Reading 'Welcher Weg hat den Vorzug?')
(1) does not meet the demand of logic for a good definition; the genetic definition is criticised. There is a remark possibly referring to Kronecker ('Kron.'), followed by '(!!!)'.
(1) in fact leads to inconveniences or difficulties ('Unzuträglichkeiten').
(2) shows the way in which the presupposition (very plausibly the consistency, 'Widerspruchslosigkeit', of the axioms) is to be proved, even though this has not yet succeeded. (2) is in any case very stimulating. (2) will perhaps also solve the problems [?] ...

This is exactly the programme of 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900): the axiomatic method is preferred, and a consistency proof for the arithmetic axioms is required. That demand became Problem 2 of the Paris problems. No computation is present to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical errors can be assessed; the page is a programmatic outline.

The limit formula in the margin is too fragmentary to check. As written ('lim_{x=0,y=0} 1/? (f(x,y)-f(x',y'))') it is incomplete, presumably a reminder of a known counterexample rather than a derivation.

results.what: Contrast of the genetic (Dedekind-Weierstrass-Cantor construction) and axiomatic (Euclid-style) foundations of the real numbers, with preference for the axiomatic one.
results.modern_name: Genetic vs. axiomatic method; axiomatic characterisation of the real numbers
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert, 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900) and Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899)

results.what: Under the axiomatic method, the existence (consistency) of the system must be proved; this has not yet been done.
Marginal example of a double limit (18th-century intuition vs. rigour)

deep.surprise_reason: These are draft notes for ideas Hilbert published in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900) and in the Paris lecture's 2nd problem. They are of mild archival interest as a draft of his genetic-vs-axiomatic argument, possibly with a jab at Kronecker, but contain nothing new.

checkable.asserts: Illustrative only (the page's own formula is illegible): the iterated limits of (x-y)/(x+y) at the origin differ (1 vs -1). This is the kind of 'intuition fails' example the margin note seems to allude to.
